clue.text: Skirt that's hitched up three hours before midday?

indicators.note: in a down clue, hitching something up lifts it, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: IX AM: nine o'clock in the morning, in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A woman hoists her long skirt early in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The skirt is long, so hitching it up sounds natural; the trick is writing 9 a.m. as IX AM.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxi is fashion shorthand for maximum, ankle-length; said of a skirt it names the garment itself.

clue.text: Cook from Serbia going to pot

indicators.note: things going to pot fall into disorder, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A chef from Serbia whose kitchen is falling apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' reads as a noun, a person from Serbia; it is the verb, and 'going to pot' doubles as a kitchen image.
explanation.definitionFit: To braise is to cook slowly in a covered pot with a little liquid.

clue.text: Talking bird

definitions.note: 'Talking' is used as a noun here: talk, conversation.
definitions.meaning: casual talk; the gerund here is the noun sense, conversation
a small songbird of the thrush family, as in stonechat and whinchat

explanation.surface: A parrot or mynah that can speak.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words read as one phrase, a bird that talks; split them and each means CHAT on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Chat is informal talking, and the chat is a family of small songbirds.

clue.text: A central point exists for God

parts.note: the nub is the central point of a matter

explanation.surface: A theological claim that a single central point exists for God.
explanation.walkthrough: The philosophical-sounding sentence is three plain pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Anubis is the jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead.

clue.text: Intricate tune with viol played

indicators.note: the tune and viol are played, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, 8 letters; 'with' joins the two words

explanation.surface: A complicated melody performed on a viol.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word after 'Intricate' is musical, which hides that the tune and viol are only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Involute means intricately complicated or entangled.

clue.text: Pastry dish with fruit rising, make a mistake and it might be flat

parts.note: a pie is a pastry dish
the date is the fruit of a palm

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upward

parts.note: to err is to make a mistake

explanation.surface: A baker's fruit pie rises, but get it wrong and it collapses flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising' and 'flat' look like baking terms for the pie; 'rising' works on the mistake, and 'flat' is a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A pied-à-terre is a small second home, often a flat kept in town.

clue.text: Express disapproval when husband tips instrument containing liquor

indicators.note: the harp holds the rum inside it
the husband sits at the tip, the end, of the instrument

parts.note: h = husband, as in genealogy abbreviations

explanation.surface: A wife tuts as her husband knocks over an instrument full of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tips' reads as knocking over; it places H at the tip of the assembled word.
explanation.definitionFit: To harrumph is to clear one's throat gruffly to show disapproval.

clue.text: Image of suspect fool's stolen

parts.note: a mug is a fool; 'fool's' = fool is, giving MUG'S
hot = stolen, as in hot goods

explanation.surface: A police photo of a fool whose goods were stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is' and belongs to MUG, leaving HOT for 'stolen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mugshot is a police photograph of a suspect's face.

clue.text: Heart of local stolen by sister I love, Church diplomat

parts.note: a nun is a sister in a religious order

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: love = O, a zero score in tennis

explanation.surface: A nun makes off with a local's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stolen by' here only joins pieces: C is taken by, and so follows, NUN.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuncio is the Pope's ambassador to a foreign government.

clue.text: Family engaged in extravagant outdoor activity

indicators.note: the family is set inside the extravagant word

parts.note: big = extravagant, as in a big gesture

explanation.surface: A family taking part in some lavish open-air pursuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged in' reads as a family taking part in something; its job is to put one piece inside another.
explanation.definitionFit: Biking is cycling, done outdoors.

clue.text: More than one newspaper sold, I suspect, after club taken over

indicators.note: a suspect version of the words is a jumbled one
the anagram comes after the club

explanation.surface: A publisher guesses several papers were sold after a football club takeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I suspect' sounds like a speaker's aside; it is the anagram indicator, and 'I' also sits in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabloids are popular newspapers; the plural matches 'more than one'.

clue.text: Walk off with sweet thing — and go too far?

definitions.meaning: literally, walk off with a biscuit
the idiom for being the most outrageous

explanation.surface: Someone pockets a sweet and is told that is overstepping the mark.
explanation.walkthrough: A biscuit is what Americans call a cookie; 'take the biscuit' is the British version of 'take the cake'.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking the biscuit is being the most outrageous, going too far.

clue.text: Sure to buy and sell supply, article going first

indicators.note: read as supple-ly, flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order
the article is placed at the front

parts.note: anagram fodder TOBUY and SELL, 9 letters; 'and' joins them

explanation.surface: A trader's instruction: be sure to deal in stock, putting one item first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' reads as the noun, goods; it is the adverb from supple (flexibly), which makes it an anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Absolutely!' is an emphatic yes, like 'sure!'.

clue.text: Loud bang originally heralding flood

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, so the start of the word, its first letter

parts.note: a rash of something is a sudden flood of it

explanation.surface: A loud bang warning that a flood is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud bang' looks like one phrase; 'Loud' is the definition, in the sense of showy.
explanation.definitionFit: Brash and loud both mean showy and vulgar, as in loud clothes.

clue.text: Way beyond some further thoughts I say!

indicators.note: the way comes beyond, after, the thoughts

parts.note: a PS, postscript, adds further thoughts to a letter

explanation.surface: A letter writer tacks on an afterthought with an exclamation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way' looks like part of the phrase 'way beyond'; it is ST, placed beyond the postscript.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Psst!' is a whisper to catch attention, like 'I say!'.

clue.text: Indian dish with duck filling half-baked roti

indicators.note: not properly baked, so the letters of roti are mixed up

parts.note: anagram fodder ROTI, rearranged as T…ORI
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, the shape of O

explanation.surface: A curry of duck with some undercooked flatbread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like the meat of the dish; it is a zero. Roti is Indian flatbread, so every word stays in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: Tandoori food is cooked in a tandoor, a clay oven.

clue.text: Vagabond, male seemingly caught?

indicators.note: the male is caught inside the trap

parts.note: what M appears caught in: a trap, a snare

explanation.surface: A drifter, a man who looks as if he has been nabbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue only hints at the trap: 'seemingly caught' says M looks snared, and TRAMP is TRAP holding M.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name someone with no home who roams from place to place.

clue.text: Fencing move I don't know: bother!

parts.note: 'pass' is what you say when you cannot answer a question

explanation.surface: A fencer admits ignorance of a move and curses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bother!' reads as an exclamation; it is the noun, trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A passado is a forward thrust in fencing with one foot advanced.

clue.text: Noble as Cockney kings and queens when stripped

indicators.note: stripping takes off the outer letters

parts.note: PEARLY kings and queens, minus P and Y

explanation.surface: A London noble who is one of the Cockney kings and queens once undressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London charity figures in suits covered in pearl buttons; stripping PEARLY of its outside letters leaves EARL.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one rank of the British peerage, which 'Noble' as a noun covers.

clue.text: Vile pants ending on floor alongside underwear for sea rover

indicators.note: as a verb, pants means is rubbish, so the letters come out wrong
the pieces sit side by side
the ending of a word is its final letter, so the ending on floor is its last letter

explanation.surface: Disgusting trousers left on the floor next to some underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' reads as trousers or underpants beside 'underwear'; it is the British slang for rubbish, working as an anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Long John Silver is the pirate in Treasure Island.

clue.text: Following spot of joyriding, crook in clink

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the crook's letters come after the spot
a spot, a small bit, of the word is its first letter

parts.note: a crook is a bend, an angle

explanation.surface: A criminal jailed after joyriding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crook' and 'clink' look like criminal and prison; crook is a bend, and clink is the definition, a metallic sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A jangle is a harsh clinking sound.

clue.text: Babies leave a mess

definitions.meaning: a brood of young animals born together to one mother
as a verb: to scatter rubbish about carelessly

explanation.surface: Babies making a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'Babies' fits a litter, one brood of young animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A litter is a brood of newborns, and littering leaves rubbish about.

clue.text: Lawyer worried about undecided strategy, ultimately

parts.note: ate = worried, as in 'what's eating you?'

indicators.note: the last letter of strategy

explanation.surface: A lawyer anxious about a strategy not yet settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worried' is the past tense of worry: ATE, as in something ate at him.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, chiefly American: one qualified to act for clients in legal matters.

clue.text: Old Tokyo, residential houses

definitions.note: Yore is a noun, time long past; 'Old' matches it only in 'days of old' = 'days of yore'.

indicators.note: the phrase houses, contains, the answer

explanation.surface: A note on old Tokyo's residential housing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' reads as buildings; it is the verb, contains.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Of yore' and 'of old' both mean of long ago.

clue.text: Where seven letters come in "dessert"?

definitions.meaning: the seven letters T to Z close the alphabet, all following the nineteenth letter
British informal word for the pudding course

explanation.surface: A spelling question about how the letters of 'dessert' fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks push you to count the letters of 'dessert', which has seven; the seven letters are the end of the alphabet, AFTER S.
explanation.definitionFit: British informal for pudding, the course that comes after the main one.

clue.text: Water seen when lid lifted from sewer

indicators.note: in a down clue, the lid is the top letter, removed

parts.note: DRAIN without its first letter D

explanation.surface: Water spotted coming out when a manhole cover is lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: The drain's lid is its top letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one form water takes, falling as drops from cloud.

clue.text: Blooming disheartened, fail test

indicators.note: loses its heart, the middle letters, leaving F and L

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam

explanation.surface: A dejected student curses after failing an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as a British mild swearword; here it means flowery.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: 'blooming' as an adjective means in flower, and the answer means made of or like flowers.

clue.text: Old country's gone to seed, so I heard

indicators.note: run down and disordered, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Rumour that a former nation has declined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So I heard' reads as a sound signal; it is the fodder. Rhodesia is now Zimbabwe and Zambia.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodesia was the former name of the country now Zimbabwe (and earlier also Zambia).
